passage:
Saturday: At the new neighbour's door, Sharmila gave Minakshi a small smile with her lips pressed together and stayed half behind her mother. “Hi!” said Minakshi. Sharmila nodded. Her mother did not say “smile properly”.
Tuesday: Minakshi waved at the lift. Sharmila's smile was the same size, but this time she said “hi” in a soft voice.
Sunday: on the compound steps with a football between them, Sharmila laughed with teeth showing. “Your turn,” she said.

qa.q: What did Sharmila do at the neighbour's door on Saturday?
qa.a: She gave Minakshi a small smile with her lips pressed together and stayed half behind her mother.

qa.q: What was Sharmila most likely feeling on Saturday, and what else might it be?
qa.a: Most likely shy with someone new, since she stayed half behind her mother and only nodded. It could also be politeness with some caution; the size of a smile does not show how much she liked Minakshi.

qa.q: How did Sharmila's mother help?
qa.a: She did not tell Sharmila to smile bigger, which gave her time to warm up in her own way.

qa.q: How might Minakshi have read the small smile on Saturday?
qa.a: She might have thought Sharmila was unfriendly, or she might have sensed shyness. She kept greeting her anyway, which helped.

grounding: A closed-mouth smile with new people is shyness or politeness; time and no forcing respect temperament.

passage:
“Listen, Aditi,” said Ishita Nani, stirring her tea. “You were nine when we went to your cousin's wedding in Jaipur. So many new faces! You gave everyone the same small smile with your lips closed and held on to my dupatta. Your mother whispered, ‘Smile properly!’ and I said, ‘Leave her, she is looking first.’ An hour later you were the one telling the little cousins how to play the game with marbles. You did not need a bigger smile. You needed time.”
Aditi grinned. “I still do that.”
“I know, beta.”

qa.q: How old was Aditi when they went to the wedding in Jaipur?
qa.a: She was nine.

qa.q: What did Ishita Nani think Aditi's small smile meant?
qa.a: That Aditi was shy and taking in many new faces, not unhappy or rude. She said Aditi was “looking first”, though she does not claim to know for certain.

qa.q: What did Ishita do that helped Aditi at the wedding?
qa.a: She told Aditi's mother to leave her alone, giving Aditi time to watch and warm up, and an hour later she was leading a game.

qa.q: How might Aditi's mother have felt when she whispered “Smile properly!”?
qa.a: Perhaps a little embarrassed that relatives would think Aditi impolite. Nani's answer shows a different way to see the smile.

grounding: A closed-mouth smile with new people carries shyness; giving time respects temperament.

passage: The photographer had ten minutes for the whole family group, and he was shouting. “Everyone, big smile! You, the boy in blue, teeth!” Pankaj had met most of these relatives only that morning. He pressed his lips together into a small, polite curve and looked at his shoes. “Bigger! Come on!” The curve got smaller. Lakshmi Maasi, standing behind him, rested a hand lightly on his shoulder. “He's smiling his way,” she told the photographer. “Take it.” The flash went off. Later, in the printed picture, Pankaj's small smile was the one that looked real.

qa.q: How long did the photographer have for the family group?
qa.a: The photographer had ten minutes for the whole family group.

qa.q: What does Pankaj's small, closed-mouth smile suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt shy among relatives he had only just met and wanted to be polite; he may also have been uncomfortable with the shouting.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi Maasi support Pankaj under the time pressure?
qa.a: She calmly told the photographer to take his natural smile, so he wasn't forced into a bigger one.

qa.q: How did the photographer see Pankaj's smile?
qa.a: The photographer saw it as not enough for a good picture, missing that pushing only made the boy shrink.

grounding: Shows a child's small closed-mouth smile with new relatives carrying shyness and politeness, and an adult refusing to force a bigger one.

passage: The new family moved into the flat below theirs in Kolkata on a Sunday. When Ma sent Anirban down with a tiffin of mishti, a boy his age opened the door. “I'm Mohit.” Anirban gave a small, closed-lipped smile, held out the tiffin and said nothing. Upstairs later, Ma nearly said, “Why can't you smile properly at people?” but stopped. Anirban had always taken a while. On Wednesday, Mohit knocked with a carrom board under his arm. By the third game Anirban was laughing out loud, teeth and all, arguing about the queen.

qa.q: What did Ma send Anirban down with?
qa.a: Ma sent him down with a tiffin of mishti.

qa.q: What was Anirban feeling when he gave Mohit a small, closed-lipped smile?
qa.a: He probably felt shy meeting someone new and was being polite; it doesn't show he disliked Mohit, only that he needed time.

qa.q: Why was Ma right to stop herself?
qa.a: Anirban always takes a while, and pushing for a bigger smile could make him more self-conscious; giving time let the real smile come.

qa.q: What might Mohit have thought after the first meeting?
qa.a: Mohit might have wondered if Anirban was unfriendly, yet he still knocked on Wednesday and gave the friendship a chance.

grounding: Shows a child's small closed-mouth smile on meeting someone new, and a parent giving time instead of forcing a bigger smile.

passage: “Gurpreet, this is Imran Sir, your new maths tutor.” “Hello, Gurpreet.” Gurpreet gave a small smile, lips closed, and slid half behind her mother's chair. “Say hello properly, beta. Give a nice big smile.” The smile flickered and went. Imran pulled his chair back a little. “No rush. I was the same at your age. Shall I just start, and you tell me when I'm wrong?” He wrote 7 + 8 = 16 on the page. Gurpreet leaned forward. “That's fifteen.” “Is it? Oh no.” This time her smile had a gap in it, a missing front tooth showing.

qa.q: What sum did Imran write on the page?
qa.a: Imran wrote 7 + 8 = 16 on the page.

qa.q: Why did Gurpreet's smile flicker and go when her mother asked for a big one?
qa.a: She likely felt shy and more self-conscious when pushed, since a forced smile can feel like being watched.

qa.q: What did Imran try instead of pushing?
qa.a: He gave her space, said he had been shy too, and made a small mistake for her to fix, letting her join in her own way.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet's mother feel seeing the gap-toothed smile?
qa.a: She might feel relieved and see that time and a gentle start work better than asking for a big smile.

grounding: Shows a child's closed-mouth smile with a new adult carrying shyness, and time and gentleness bringing a real smile.

passage:
My name is Ishita, and last summer we moved to a building in Kochi where I knew nobody. The first evening, the lady from upstairs, Mrs Elizabeth, came down with a plate of banana fritters. Mummy nudged me. "Say hello properly, smile nicely!"

I gave my small smile, lips shut, and looked at the fritters. Mummy sighed, but Mrs Elizabeth just said, "Take your time, I'm not going anywhere."

She came again on Sunday, and again after that. By the third plate I was telling her about my rabbit, and my smile had teeth in it.

qa.q: What did Mrs Elizabeth bring down the first evening?
qa.a: A plate of banana fritters.

qa.q: What was Ishita most likely feeling behind the small, closed-mouth smile that first evening?
qa.a: Shyness and politeness with a stranger in a new place rather than delight; looking at the fritters instead of her face suggests Ishita felt a bit nervous 🙂

qa.q: How could Mummy handle Ishita's shy smile differently?
qa.a: Instead of pushing for a bigger smile, give Ishita time, as Mrs Elizabeth did, and let the friendliness grow over several visits.

qa.q: How does Mrs Elizabeth read Ishita's small smile?
qa.a: She seems to see it as shyness, not rudeness, and calmly keeps visiting until Ishita is ready to open up.

grounding: It is a child's look back at giving a small closed-mouth smile to a new neighbour out of shyness, and being given time rather than pushed.
